title: Wiring Capital to Compute
gist: A compute-economics operator uses the cancelled ~1GW Stargate expansion in Abilene to argue the US AI buildout is bottlenecked not by capital but by missing financial instruments: there is no standardized offtake contract, rating methodology, or securitization channel for frontier compute, so nearly every external dollar still resolves back to a handful of hyperscaler balance sheets. He contrasts this with China's state-coordinated EDWC buildout — faster to power but ~80% idle capacity — and warns that with big tech at a third of the S&P 500, index and pension portfolios already hold compute risk that was never priced or underwritten.

insights.claim: Stargate was announced days after Trump's 2025 inauguration with SoftBank's Masayoshi Son, Oracle's Larry Ellison and OpenAI's Sam Altman pledging $500 billion over a four-year horizon — but unlike Apollo-scale precedents, the federal government was neither underwriter nor customer, leaving private capital alone to fund GPUs, land and power.
insights.speaker: Daniel Painter
insights.so_what: White House endorsement carried no credit support, so the project's viability always rested on private counterparty risk — a distinction to apply to every future 'national AI project' headline.
insights.quote: Private capital alone was set to accelerate machine intelligence through GPUs, land, and power, with the White House only lending its podium.
insights.locator: Abilene was the intended flagship

insights.claim: The Abilene campus was planned at an initial 1.2 gigawatts — enough for roughly a million homes — with nearly another gigawatt slated to be added; financing was secured and papers drawn up, but the expansion was cancelled and full energization slipped from March 2026 to as late as mid-2027.
insights.speaker: Daniel Painter
insights.so_what: Concrete evidence that announced gigawatt pipelines are not contracted capacity — discount headline GW figures and track energization dates instead.
insights.locator: Today, the grounds of Stargate's flagship site

insights.claim: The Abilene expansion died from deal structure rather than construction: it leaned on just two counterparties to shoulder compute infrastructure risk, and when OpenAI's internal cash-flow forecasts moved far enough, the risk-allocation structure could not absorb the swing.
insights.speaker: Daniel Painter
insights.so_what: The dominant failure mode for AI infra is a tenant forecast revision, not a power or supply-chain shortfall — monitor lab demand guidance as the leading indicator for data-center capex cancellations.
insights.quote: when OpenAI’s internal cash-flow forecasts moved far enough, the deal’s structure could not absorb the swing
insights.locator: Abilene leaned heavily on two counterparties

insights.claim: Abilene's joint venture had Crusoe as developer-operator raising a $7.1 billion construction loan from a J.P. Morgan-led consortium for the campus's second phase on top of an earlier $2.3 billion facility, secured against Oracle's eventual ownership of the cluster with OpenAI as planned lessee — making roughly $9.4 billion of debt financeable almost solely on faith in OpenAI's single tenancy.
insights.speaker: Daniel Painter
insights.so_what: Construction lenders to AI campuses are taking concentrated single-tenant credit risk several layers removed from the borrower — a place to look for mispriced credit.
insights.quote: This was financeable almost solely on faith in OpenAI’s single tenancy, abstracted under several layers.
insights.locator: Stargate's Abilene deployment was structured as a joint venture

insights.claim: Reading the episode as 'Stargate failed' is wrong: the main Abilene campus still serves OpenAI compute and what collapsed was specifically the multi-gigawatt expansion arrangement between OpenAI, Oracle and Crusoe.
insights.speaker: Daniel Painter
insights.so_what: Distinguish operating compute from cancelled expansion when assessing AI capex headlines — the signal is in incremental capacity, not in whether flagship sites run.
insights.quote: However, it is a mistake to interpret this by simply saying that “Stargate failed,”
insights.locator: However, it is a mistake to interpret this

insights.claim: The compute buildout sits awkwardly between corporate finance and project finance — it carries the risk profile of the former and the scale of the latter, adding billions of debt to a balance sheet — so no existing capital-conversion template fits the asset class cleanly.
insights.speaker: Daniel Painter
insights.so_what: Until a template exists, every AI infra deal is bespoke and slow — a structural cap on how fast external capital can be deployed regardless of appetite.
insights.quote: there is currently no capital-conversion machinery—no templates—that fit this asset class cleanly
insights.locator: The compute buildout is awkwardly positioned

insights.claim: A compute asset is several assets with different lifespans stacked together: shell, land, substation and cooling can last decades but are repriced by the chip cycle as substation sizings and cooling standards designed for one hardware generation lose value against the next, while GPUs and their memory and storage are repriced by product cycles rather than ordinary depreciation.
insights.speaker: Daniel Painter
insights.so_what: Even the 'durable' layer of a data center is exposed to the chip cycle, so long-dated data-center debt is less insulated from GPU obsolescence than it looks.
insights.locator: A compute infrastructure asset is actually several assets

insights.claim: The efficient structure would slice a supercomputer by layer — long-dated debt on the shell and aggressive amortization against the silicon — which happens ad hoc today but is neither standardized nor predictable, and newer deployments increasingly demand codevelopment and therefore parallel financing of all layers.
insights.speaker: Daniel Painter
insights.so_what: A tranched shell-versus-silicon financing standard is the obvious product gap; whoever standardizes it captures the intermediation fee on ~$1.5tn of demand.
insights.locator: It is difficult to fund data centers as one long-dated asset

insights.claim: Mature infrastructure finance prices risk by spreading it over many uncorrelated customers, but frontier compute inverts this by building for a single dominant offtaker that is young, conventionally unprofitable and prone to wildly revising its own demand forecasts.
insights.speaker: Daniel Painter
insights.so_what: Single-offtaker concentration is the defining credit weakness of AI infra; diversity of contracted offtakers is the metric that separates durable from fragile projects.
insights.locator: For the buyer, mature infrastructure financing prices risk

insights.claim: When OpenAI's forecast moved on Abilene, no instrument existed to absorb the change: there was no termination pricing to compensate the asset for a demand revision, no resale market where a departing tenant’s capacity could clear, and no demand insurance to bridge the gap.
insights.speaker: Daniel Painter
insights.so_what: The three missing products — termination pricing, secondary capacity markets, demand insurance — are the specific instruments to watch for as signs the asset class is maturing.
insights.quote: There was no termination pricing to compensate the asset for the demand revision, no resale market where a departing tenant’s capacity could clear, and no demand insurance to bridge the gap.
insights.locator: When OpenAI's forecast moved

insights.claim: Standardized compute offtake contracts that tranche and distribute risk, rating methodologies purpose-built for frontier compute, and securitization channels for assets under construction do not exist — compute only has fragments of such instruments used improvisationally, deal by deal.
insights.speaker: Daniel Painter
insights.so_what: First movers in compute ratings methodology and construction-phase securitization would unlock institutional demand; their absence is the binding constraint on the buildout.
insights.locator: Standardized compute offtake contracts

insights.claim: Compute is inherently harder to finance than power infrastructure because of aggressive hardware obsolescence, buyer concentration, unstable demand shocks and export controls, and no party can justify or explain total cost recovery for an AI buildout the way they readily can for a power plant.
insights.speaker: Daniel Painter
insights.so_what: Analogies to utility-style contracted infrastructure understate AI infra risk; demand a materially higher risk premium than power-plant project debt.
insights.locator: The closest existing template is the financing of a single power plant

insights.claim: Morgan Stanley projects the global data center buildout at roughly $2.9 trillion through 2028, of which hyperscalers can fund only half even deploying their entire balance sheets — meaning some $1.5 trillion must come reliably and repeatably from external capital while each deal is still negotiated and priced from scratch.
insights.speaker: Daniel Painter
insights.so_what: The $1.5tn external requirement is the size of the addressable market for new compute-finance instruments — and the size of the shortfall if standardization does not arrive.
insights.locator: According to Morgan Stanley

insights.claim: The United States holds roughly 40% of the world's equity and a comparable share of fixed income — the largest concentration of capital ever assembled — so the binding constraint on the AI buildout is not money but the absence of bankable assets.
insights.speaker: Daniel Painter
insights.so_what: Bet on the instrument layer, not the capital layer: bottleneck relief comes from legal and rating standardization, not from more dry powder.
insights.quote: Capital is abundant, but bankable assets are not.
insights.locator: The question of interest is not whether America has money

insights.claim: Compute capital has shifted away from straightforward balance-sheet spending toward experimental structures — joint ventures, long-term leases, private credit, offtake mixes and securitized lease cash flows sold to institutional investors — but most of these only tighten the link between hyperscalers, non-bank lenders and insurers rather than inject new capital.
insights.speaker: Daniel Painter
insights.so_what: The proliferation of exotic AI-infra structures is a demand signal, but also a contagion channel linking insurers and private credit to a handful of tech credits.
insights.locator: The Symptoms

insights.claim: In the year before its IPO, roughly 62% of CoreWeave's revenue came from Microsoft and another 15% from its second-largest customer, and later deals including large OpenAI commitments broadened the customer base without meaningfully diluting that concentration.
insights.speaker: Daniel Painter
insights.so_what: Neocloud equity and debt is a levered derivative of two or three hyperscaler credits; treat customer-concentration disclosure as the key risk line in neocloud filings.
insights.locator: Companies like CoreWeave have emerged

insights.claim: Nearly every external dollar entering AI infrastructure today does so through a structure whose credit ultimately resolves back to the same handful of hyperscaler names, legally separating risks that remain economically correlated — a pattern the author likens to pre-2008 instruments that appeared to diversify risk while concentrating it.
insights.speaker: Daniel Painter
insights.so_what: Apparent diversification across AI-infra vehicles is illusory; stress-test portfolios for simultaneous drawdown across neoclouds, private credit and hyperscaler debt.
insights.quote: it eerily resembles past moments in financial history, such as the 2008 financial crisis, when instruments appeared to diversify risk while actually concentrating it behind the scenes
insights.locator: When capital flows between a few giants who self-finance

themes.theme: China's Planned Buildout and Its Failure Modes

insights.claim: Beijing will spend roughly $295 billion over five years on a grid of nationalized AI data centers and plans to produce 80% of its AI chips domestically by 2028.
insights.speaker: Daniel Painter
insights.so_what: Sets the scale marker for state-directed compute capex and the deadline against which Chinese domestic accelerator progress should be judged.
insights.locator: China is Eating the Gap

insights.claim: China's Eastern Data Western Computing initiative, launched in 2022, organizes compute around eight national hubs and ten data center clusters to match eastern demand to western power and land, where electricity prices run 40% below those in the east.
insights.speaker: Daniel Painter
insights.so_what: A 40% power-cost differential is the core economic logic of China's siting strategy — and a benchmark for US siting arbitrage between load centers and cheap-power regions.
insights.locator: This should be seen in light of the Eastern Data Western Computing

insights.claim: Of more than 500 data center projects announced under EDWC, only 150 were completed by end-2024, roughly 80% of new capacity sits idle per local reports, more than 100 projects have been scrapped, and poster-child province Guizhou remains near the bottom of provincial GDP rankings with heavy debts and big-data corruption problems.
insights.speaker: Daniel Painter
insights.so_what: Hard evidence against the 'China is simply winning the compute race' narrative — Chinese announced capacity converts to utilized capacity at a very low rate.
insights.locator: Under the EDWC, more than 500 data center projects were announced

insights.claim: Chinese compute projects are underwritten against state priorities rather than corporate cash flows, with provincial governments allocating land to plan while state-directed banks disburse funds at CCP discretion, and operators in Zhengzhou giving compute vouchers away outright to conjure demand for capacity built ahead of any customer.
insights.speaker: Daniel Painter
insights.so_what: China's speed advantage comes from removing the offtake test entirely, so Chinese capacity data says little about real AI demand there.
insights.quote: in Zhengzhou, operators have gone as far as giving compute vouchers away to conjure demand for capacity built ahead of any customer
insights.locator: China has not forgone the counterparts

insights.claim: Beijing's response to EDWC overbuild — utilization minimums, bans on locally funded and small-scale facilities, and purchase mandates set before construction begins — amounts to the state manually reconstructing the price signals and underwriting standards a functioning market would supply.
insights.speaker: Daniel Painter
insights.so_what: Central planning does not escape the underwriting problem, it just relocates it — a reason to doubt calls for a nationalized US buildout.
insights.quote: The state is manually reconstructing the price signals and underwriting standards of a functioning market.
insights.locator: Beijing's response to this has been to institute utilization minimums

insights.claim: China's most binding constraint is its 80% domestic chip target: if Huawei and other domestic producers cannot manufacture high-performance accelerators at scale, US export controls bite hard, and because domestic accelerators deliver less performance per watt, abundant western Chinese electricity buys less intelligence per gigawatt.
insights.speaker: Daniel Painter
insights.so_what: Performance-per-watt, not gigawatts or dollars, is the metric that decides the US-China compute race — watch Huawei accelerator yield and efficiency disclosures.
insights.quote: domestic accelerators deliver less performance per watt, so abundant electricity buys less intelligence per gigawatt
insights.locator: The most binding problem facing China's buildout

insights.claim: China's high-speed rail program — more track laid in fifteen years than the rest of the world combined, using the same provincial land allocation and state-bank credit underwritten against national priorities — was a dress rehearsal for the AI push, and it left lines built to political rather than ridership logic with debt buried in local-government financing vehicles.
insights.speaker: Daniel Painter
insights.so_what: The HSR template predicts where Chinese compute debt will surface: opaque provincial vehicles, with faster obsolescence than rail assets.
insights.quote: Compute will prove a harder problem than rail: the technology obsolesces faster, and its demand curve is far less understood.
insights.locator: The high-speed rail buildout

themes.theme: Systemic Exposure and the Rail-Era Precedent

insights.claim: US securities markets were built by the infrastructure they funded — no deep market for industrial securities existed when the first rail promoters began laying track, and standardized paper, ratings, reporting and exchanges were developed while the tracks went down.
insights.speaker: Daniel Painter
insights.so_what: Implies compute-finance standards will be forged during, not before, the buildout — creating a window for whoever writes the first templates.
insights.quote: Standardized paper, ratings, reporting, and, later, exchanges were developed while tracks were being laid.
insights.locator: Historically, America has developed the institutions

insights.claim: The Panic of 1873 began in railroad finance with Jay Cooke's failure, yet the crash did not end the rail buildout — the financial technologies the boom had forged, standardized bonds, ratings and disclosure, carried the next construction wave on sounder terms.
insights.speaker: Daniel Painter
insights.so_what: A compute credit event would not invalidate AI demand, but it would reset who finances it and on what documentation — position for the post-panic standard-setters.
insights.quote: A financial panic caused by compute would not mean the buildout was a mistake, the same way the dot-com bubble does not invalidate internet shopping or telecommunications.
insights.locator: Looking to the rail era once more

insights.claim: With the largest technology companies at roughly a third of the S&P 500, pension funds and retail index portfolios already carry concentrated compute exposure they never underwrote, and no instrument exists that would let a rules-bound pension fund underwrite a data center directly, price its own tranche of risk and be compensated for bearing it.
insights.speaker: Daniel Painter
insights.so_what: Passive investors are unpaid holders of AI buildout risk; the arrival of a direct compute-tranche instrument would be a genuine repricing event for both index and private allocations.
insights.quote: The hyperscalers can take buildout risk on the chin in a way a rules-bound pension fund cannot.
insights.locator: The malady of capital only reaching deployment

insights.claim: Unlike dot-com-era fiber-optic cable that stayed useful for decades, an AI buildout done with the wrong equipment gets no second life, because AI infrastructure combines the capital intensity of the electrical grid, the depreciation clock of consumer electronics and the strategic stakes of aerospace.
insights.speaker: Daniel Painter
insights.so_what: The standard 'overbuilt fiber eventually got used' consolation does not transfer to GPUs — recovery value in a bust is far lower than telecom analogies imply.
insights.quote: It has the capital intensity of the electrical grid, the depreciation clock of consumer electronics, and the strategic stakes of aerospace.
insights.locator: Every few generations, some cohort has stood present

insights.claim: The author's prescription is a bankable rather than nationalized buildout — pouring more capital onto the fire will not suffice, and every month American markets fail to convert capital into buildout progress strengthens the chorus calling for state control.
insights.speaker: Daniel Painter
insights.so_what: Watch for US policy drift toward direct state financing of compute as the political consequence of continued private-market failure — a regime change for who earns the returns.
insights.quote: The solution is a bankable buildout, not a nationalized one.
insights.locator: The Strategic Test
